Intrinsic value and margin of safety

Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a business is worth based on its cash flows, assets or earnings power. Margin of safety means buying only when market price sits meaningfully below that careful estimate — so mistakes hurt less.

Estimates are not oracle prices

Different reasonable investors can produce different values from the same filings. Small changes in growth or discount assumptions move results a lot.

Treat any single “fair value” number — especially from strangers online — as a hypothesis to test, not a fact.

What margin of safety is for

If your analysis might be wrong (it might), paying a discounted price leaves room for bad luck, slower growth or accounting surprises.

Thin margins of safety turn investing into a requirement that you are nearly perfect. That is a fragile plan.

Practical habits on PSX

Use filings, conservative assumptions, and peer checks. Prefer businesses you understand. Avoid leverage that forces you to sell at the worst time.

Document why the price looked attractive when you bought. Hindsight rewrites memory otherwise.

After the purchase

Your wealth change comes from dividends and the difference between sale proceeds and what you paid, including fees. Record those facts carefully.

PSX Tracker focuses on that personal ledger while you keep refining how you estimate value.

The idea, without the costume

Margin of safety is the gap between what you think a business is worth and the price the market asks. You want the price to be lower, by enough that you can be somewhat wrong and still not be ruined. Benjamin Graham wrote about this as a discipline of conservatism. This page is a plain explanation of the discipline. It is not a complete copying of his books, and it is not a formula that prints a fair value.

The gap exists only if your estimate of value is independent of the price. If you take the price, multiply it by a story, and call the result value, there is no gap. There is a circle. Start from the business: what it earns, what it owns, what it owes, and what a cautious person would believe those figures will do.

A large gap does not make you safe. It makes the odds less brutal if your estimate was nearly right. If your estimate was fantasy, the gap was fantasy too.

Value is a range

Use more than one blunt measure. What do the assets look like after a haircut to receivables and inventory you would not want to collect yourself? What does a conservative multiple of average earnings say, using a run of years rather than the best year? What does the dividend stream look like if you refuse to assume it grows?

Where those approaches cluster, you have a range. Where they scatter, you do not understand the business well enough to claim a value. The honest output is “I do not know,” which is a reason not to size a large position.

Write the assumptions next to the range. A change in the sugar price, the policy rate, the gas tariff, or the tax rate can move the range by more than the margin you thought you had. If the thesis depends on a policy that can be revised in a budget speech, the margin needs to be wide or the position needs to be small.

The market’s job is to offer a price, not to be right

Prices move because other people are forced to, bored, frightened, or excited. You do not need a theory of their mood. You need a price that is attractive against the range you wrote down when you were calm. If the price is not attractive, you do nothing. Doing nothing is the usual correct action.

A falling price is not automatically a larger margin of safety. The value may have fallen with the price, because the business got worse. Re-read the latest accounts before you add. The phrase “it is cheaper now” skips that re-reading and has funded a lot of losses.

A rising price can erase the margin while the business stays fine. That is a reason to be careful about adding, not automatically a reason to sell a business you still understand. Selling and buying have costs. The margin is a buying discipline first.

Position size is part of the margin

Being right and being wiped out can happen together if the position was so large that an ordinary error became a personal crisis. The margin of safety in the price does not replace a limit on how much of your savings one name can be. Decide the limit when you are calm.

Averaging down is only coherent when the value is intact and the new price improves the gap. Averaging down because you cannot bear the red number is how a small mistake becomes the whole portfolio. The ledger will show the new, lower average. It will not show that you broke your limit. You have to write the limit somewhere you will see it.

Diversification across a handful of understood businesses is another kind of margin: against the chance that one range was wrong. A long list of half-understood bargains is not that. It is a second job you will not do.

How to keep the practice in the tracker

You can note, in your own words, the range you estimated and the price you paid. Months later the unrealized figure tells you how the market moved, not whether your range was right. Revisit the range when new accounts come out. Update the note. Do not update the story to match whatever the price did.

Nothing in PSX Tracker calculates intrinsic value. Be wary of any tool that offers a single precise fair-value number with false confidence. A range you built from the annual report, with the assumptions visible, is slower and better.

This is not advice to buy cheap stocks, and it is not a claim that Graham’s older numerical rules still fit every Pakistani company. It is an invitation to pay less than a cautious estimate, on purpose, and to admit when you do not have one.

Common questions

What is a margin of safety?

The gap between what you estimate a business is worth and the price you pay. It is a cushion for being wrong, not a guarantee.

Can a model give an exact fair value?

No. Inputs are estimates. Treat the result as a range you can defend, then compare it with the market price.

Is this Benjamin Graham’s method as a checklist to copy?

It is a conceptual introduction. It is not a complete investing system and not advice to buy or sell.
